# Understanding how Glassfrog failures are reported

When a `glassfrog` command fails, you don't see a bare HTTP status or a wall of raw response body. You see one diagnostic — a cause, a category, and a next step — rendered in the same output format you asked for, and your shell sees a distinct exit code for what kind of failure it was. That consistency is produced by a three-stage pipeline: **extract** the failure into a typed error, **normalize** it into one diagnostic shape, and **render** it in the selected format. This document explains why the pipeline is shaped that way, what alternatives were weighed, and where it deliberately stops.

## The pipeline in one picture

1. **Extract** (API Error Extraction) — the transport layer sends one request and hands back a generic outcome; a pure interpretation step refines a 4xx/5xx into a typed error carrying the authoritative HTTP status, the API's own detail, and the raw body.
2. **Normalize** (Diagnostic Normalization) — one function turns any failure — typed API error, transport failure, decode failure, auth or config error — into a single `Diagnostic` value: `{cause, category, next step}`, the same shape regardless of family.
3. **Render** (Output-Aware Failure Rendering) — the diagnostic is rendered in the resolved `--output` format: a structured envelope on stdout under `json`/`yaml`, a human diagnostic on stderr under `full`/`compact`.

The exit code is derived from the diagnostic's category by the single Exit-Code Convention mapper, so the code and the message can never disagree.

## Why a failed call becomes a typed, legible error

The transport layer sends exactly one request and, on a 4xx/5xx, hands back a generic, uncategorized outcome: a status, headers, and a raw body. It never interprets which *kind* of failure the status represents — that is a separate job. The problem this addresses is opaque failures: from a raw status and body, a caller (or an AI agent acting for you) can't tell what went wrong or what to do.

So the CLI refines that generic outcome into one structured error carrying the API's authoritative status, the API's own detail, and the raw body and headers. The Glassfrog API serves every 4xx/5xx as an RFC 9457 Problem Details document (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`), so there is a documented, human-meaningful cause to extract — which is what turns "status 404" into "Not Found, here is why."

Two alternatives were rejected. **Parsing the body inside the single-send transport step** would blur the clean line between "send and report what came back" and "interpret what came back." **Parsing in the presentation layer** would deny a non-interactive caller (a script, a test) the typed error and put wire-body parsing in a layer whose job is to display, not parse. The chosen approach refines the generic outcome in a dedicated, pure step that *wraps* the original — so the raw status, headers, and body stay reachable, and the interpretation is reusable by any caller.

## Why the HTTP status wins, and the body is read best-effort

Two realities shaped how the body is read. Gateways and proxies sometimes return empty bodies, HTML error pages, or non-conformant Problem Details — so the body can't be trusted to be readable. And an RFC 9457 body can carry its own `status` member that disagrees with the actual HTTP status on the wire.

The design treats the HTTP status as authoritative and parses the body best-effort. Requiring an `application/problem+json` content type before parsing was rejected — gateways send problem bodies with varying or absent content types, so gating on the header would throw away readable detail the API did send. Trusting the body's self-reported `status` was rejected — a body claiming `401` on a `403` response would mislead anyone branching on the code. So the interpretation reads the documented shape regardless of declared type; when the body is valid it surfaces `detail`/`title`/`type` and preserves the raw body, and when it is absent, non-JSON, or missing members it derives a usable detail from the HTTP status.

The step is deliberately *total*: it always produces a typed error and never crashes on a junk body — because the input is already a failure, and making it *also* crash would recreate the opacity it exists to remove. A subtle consequence: the error records whether the detail is the API's own words or a status-derived fallback, so a synthesized phrase is never presented to you as though the API had said it.

## Why one normalizer produces one diagnostic shape

Historically, the category came from one function and the cause and next step from another — two independent chains tied together only at the point of printing. They could drift in arm order, and the next stage (format-aware rendering) needs a *structured value*, not a pre-printed string.

The consolidation introduces a single normalizer that, for each failure family, computes the category, cause, and next step **together from the same matched error** — so they cannot disagree. The alternative, leaving the two chains split and having the renderer call both, was rejected: it pushes the "one consistent shape" obligation downstream and keeps the exact drift hazard the consolidation removes. The result is one place to reason about every failure family (auth, transport, non-2xx-by-status, decode, base-URL, config, format, and a fail-safe fallback), and a clean structured value for the renderer to consume.

The normalizer is also *total*: it never panics and always returns a diagnostic; an unrecognized error maps to the runtime-error fallback (exit `1`, never `0`). Genuine panics that never reach it are caught by the process-level panic-recover safety net — the normalizer adds no competing internal-diagnostic path.

## Why a decode failure counts as an API error, not an internal one

One deliberate reclassification rides along with the normalizer. A 2xx response whose body won't decode used to map to the internal-error code `1`. It now maps to the general **API-error code `3`**. The reasoning: the call succeeded at the wire but the API returned an unreadable shape — that is an API-exchange problem, not a CLI bug. The result is a coherent split: exit `3` means "the API's fault" (a non-2xx *or* an unreadable 2xx), and exit `1` means "our fault" (a panic, a render-template failure, the fallback). Render-template failures stay at `1` — they are genuinely CLI-internal — so the split sharpens rather than blurs. The cause wording is unchanged ("the API response did not match the expected shape — this may be an API change; report it"); only the category moved. This supersedes the prior decode-classification precedent.

## Why permission and rate-limit failures get their own codes and next steps

Beyond a readable message, the CLI assigns an exit code by *kind* of failure, so a script or agent can branch on it. The exit-code convention reserved distinct codes for permission and rate-limit failures; the normalizer fills them by branching on the status in the one shared classification step every command funnels through: `401`/`403` → the permission code `4`, `429` → the rate-limit code `5`, everything else → the generic API code `3`.

The next steps were then refined so the recovery action is specific rather than generic:

- **`401`** points at verifying the configured API token; **`403`** points at your identity possibly lacking the required role membership — a split of the old single combined hint, because the two failures need different fixes.
- **`429`** points at the rate-limit reset window (read from the `Retry-After` / `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers already on the error) rather than a bare "retry later."

A deliberate consequence of filling the reserved codes: responses that once exited with the generic code now exit `4` (for `401`/`403`) or `5` (for `429`). That is intended — it fills reserved, published codes rather than renumbering anything — but it is an observable change for anyone scripting on the old generic code, which is why it is called out rather than slipped in silently.

There is a careful ownership boundary around `429`: rate-limit handling owns *retrying* a throttled request within bounded caps; this pipeline owns *classifying* the `429` that finally survives, and never waits. And a related sibling capability, guarded writes, adds one more category on the same seam — a stale write (`412`) maps to its own code `7` with a re-read-and-retry next step (see [How guarded writes prevent clobbering](how-guarded-writes-prevent-clobbering.md)).

## Why failures render in the format you asked for

For a long time a failure was always printed to stderr as plain text, whatever `--output` you selected — a documented interim gap. Output-aware rendering closes it by extending the single failure chokepoint (the same seam the normalizer feeds) into a format-aware reporter, rather than adding a parallel renderer. Extending the one chokepoint keeps a single rendering contract and reaches every command-execution failure; the signature change makes the compiler enforce that no call site is missed. The alternative — wrapping only the generic success-dispatch — would have left the paginated reads emitting plain-text failures under `json`/`yaml`, a silent half-fix.

Three decisions shape what you see:

- **Channel by format.** Under `json`/`yaml` the failure is rendered as the unified error envelope on **stdout** — the channel an agent parses, so success and failure read the same way. Under `full`/`compact` the cause-plus-next-step diagnostic goes to **stderr**, byte-for-byte as before. The exit code is the same in both.
- **The next step is its own field.** Because the operator is often an AI agent reading the recovery action programmatically, the structured envelope carries `next_step` as a distinct, parseable element (`omitempty`, so it's absent when there is no reliable recovery), rather than folded into the message. The envelope also carries a `kind` (a 1:1 map from the category), and the API's `status` and raw `body` when present — the body only when it is valid JSON, so a malformed upstream body never suppresses the diagnostic.
- **The partial-walk nuance.** A paginated read can fail mid-walk after some pages already rendered — under a structured format, a partial `{data:[…]}` document is already on stdout. Rather than emit a second document there (breaking "one document per channel") or suppress the data already gathered, the partial document stays on stdout, the incompleteness note stays a plain-text line on stderr, and the non-zero exit code is the authoritative failure signal. This is the one place a structured run emits non-structured text on the secondary channel, and it is deliberate.

## How the cause reaches you without leaking secrets

The rendered failure can never carry your authentication token. The interpretation reads only the *response* side — the status, headers, and body the API replied with — and the token is a *request* header, structurally out of reach on this path. The normalizer produces token-free cause and next-step text for every family, and the structured renderer adds nothing to the values it is handed. This invariant is load-bearing and tested arm-for-arm.

## Risk landscape

The dominant safety concern is that the interpretation might crash or return nothing on a malformed body — the empty, HTML, or truncated bodies gateways commonly produce — re-opacifying the very failure it exists to make legible. The control is structural: every stage is *total* by design, degrading to a status-derived fallback rather than failing, with the empty/HTML/missing-member cases pinned by tests. The structured renderer keeps the same discipline — it buffers then writes, so a render that cannot complete leaves nothing partial on stdout and maps to the runtime-error code, never a silent success.

A second concern is shared with the rate-limit story: a `429` that this pipeline classifies but never retries; the blast radius of an unhandled throttle is the whole organization (the limit is per-org). This pipeline neither amplifies nor fully resolves that exposure — it preserves the rate-limit headers intact for the retry layer and classifies the survivor. Smaller, well-controlled concerns round out the picture: a status-derived fallback mistaken for the API's own words (closed by the provenance marker); a message with no next step (closed by the per-class hints, with honest omission where none applies); a classification-ordering bug letting `401`/`403` fall through (closed by branching on status before the generic arm); and a missed render call site leaking plain text under a structured format (closed by the compiler-enforced signature change).

## Design boundaries

Understanding what this pipeline deliberately does *not* do clarifies where it sits among its neighbors:

- **It does not send requests or retry.** The single-send layer owns sending; rate-limit handling owns retrying and backing off on a `429`. This pipeline extracts, classifies, and renders — it never waits.
- **It does not re-parse the raw body twice.** Extraction produces the typed error once; normalization and rendering read that, not the wire body again.
- **It does not decide the exit code itself.** The category feeds the single Exit-Code Convention mapper, which owns the code — so rendering and the code stay derived from one value and cannot disagree.
- **It does not translate a `403` into "not available on your plan."** Plan-availability interpretation is a separate concern (Unsignalled Plan Limits); this pipeline carries the `403` generically so that capability can build on it without overlap.
- **It does not render usage errors or the invalid-format-selector error in the structured format.** Those fail before a command executes — at or around the point the format is resolved — so a reliable format isn't available to render into; they keep their plain-text path.
- **It does not render successful results, or fabricate a cause or next step the failure doesn't support.** A confidently wrong cause rendered as clean JSON is more dangerous than an honest, status-derived one.

These boundaries rest on one assumption worth surfacing: the Glassfrog API is taken to serve every 4xx/5xx as a conformant RFC 9457 Problem Details document. The CLI relies on that contract for the rich case while degrading gracefully whenever a non-conformant body arrives — which is exactly why the best-effort parse and the status fallback exist.
